cur:catacombs-louvre-traditio-legis-ma29.summary: Against a backdrop of city walls and gates, Christ stands at the centre on the hill of paradise, handing the scroll of the Law to Peter, while the other apostles approach from both sides in a stately procession. The 'city-gate' background evokes the heavenly Jerusalem into which the apostles – and the deceased – are received.
facts: Commons records that it came from the mausoleum of the Anicii beneath St Peter's in the Vatican.
The Traditio Legis, Christ giving the law to Peter, was a favourite theme of late-4th-century Roman art.

cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-sh.summary: At the centre of the chest the Lamb of God stands on the mountain of Paradise, from which the four rivers flow between palm trees, an image of Christ the sacrificed and victorious Lamb. To the left and right, in more damaged reliefs, Christ performs the miracles of Cana, with its tall water jars, and the multiplication of the loaves. On the lid two flocks of three sheep approach a central Christogram with Alpha and omega.
facts: Like the Christ Enthroned sarcophagus beside it, it was reconstituted with the help of old drawings by Louis Antoine de Ruffi and Joseph Marchand.
French Wikipedia notes a Latinised rho in the Christogram on the lid, flanked by a capital Alpha and a lower-case omega.
cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-sh.notes: Christ appears both symbolically as the Lamb and, in damaged form, in the two miracle scenes.
cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-sh.original_title: Sarcophage des brebis et des cerfs

cur:manuscripts-lorsch-gospels-christ-in.summary: Christ, beardless and youthful with a golden cross-nimbus, sits frontally on a cushioned throne against a deep blue disc, blessing and holding a jewelled book. Around him a broad ring holds medallions of the four evangelist symbols and small busts of prophets, while gold capitals above and below declare that the four living creatures proclaim the sacred gifts of Christ. It is the central image of one of the most sumptuous books made for Charlemagne's court.
facts: The Lorsch Gospels is now divided: Matthew, Mark and the prefatory pages are in Alba Iulia, Romania, Luke and John in the Vatican Library, and the ivory covers in the Vatican Museums and the Victoria and Albert Museum.

It was recorded in Lorsch Abbey's library catalogue of 830 as a Gospel book 'written in gold ... with ivory tablets'; in 1622, during the Thirty Years' War, it was taken from Heidelberg and broken in two to make it easier to sell.
The German Wikipedia notes that its Majestas Domini influenced later Ottonian painting, for example the Majestas of the Gero Codex.
cur:manuscripts-lorsch-gospels-christ-in.notes: Folio not given by the Commons source (a facsimile plate); the miniature is usually cited as fol. 18v of the Alba Iulia volume.

walters:27.565.summary: On one face of this small, roughly worked stone block the Lamb of God strides forward in flat raised relief, his head ringed by a nimbus and a cross raised beside him. The Lamb's eyes were once filled with lead, which still remains. The block, carved differently on each of its four sides, shows how the symbol of Christ the sacrificed and victorious Lamb was woven into the fabric of church buildings.
facts: The Walters notes that each of the four faces carries a different ornament, and that holes at top and bottom were used for attachment.
Lead was used to pick out details such as the Lamb's eyes; only the lead in the eyes survives.
walters:27.565.notes: Dated broadly 9th–11th century by the museum; its 'Romanesque' style label is the museum's. Image viewed on the Walters image server.
